Family Health

Smell and taste changes after COVID-19: recovery, research and practical help

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A change in smell or taste can linger after the rest of a COVID-19 illness improves. Understanding which sense is affected and how it changes daily life is more useful than relying on a single recovery deadline or headline statistic.

Smell, taste and flavour are related but different

After COVID-19, coffee may seem almost odourless, a familiar meal may lack flavour, or a previously pleasant smell may become unpleasant. Changes can be partial or complete and can affect smell, taste or both. They can follow a mild infection as well as a more severe illness.

Taste detects qualities such as sweetness, saltiness, sourness, bitterness and umami. Smell supplies much of the aroma that helps distinguish foods. Flavour combines these signals with texture and temperature, so food tasting bland does not by itself establish that the taste system has stopped working.

A useful description is what you can and cannot perceive: for example, whether you still notice that sugar is sweet but cannot recognise the aroma of an orange. This helps a clinician separate altered smell from a true taste problem without dismissing either experience.

Loss and distortion do not feel the same

Anosmia means absent smell, while hyposmia means reduced smell. With parosmia, an actual odour is perceived differently; familiar foods can smell burnt, chemical or rotten. Phantosmia means sensing an odour when no corresponding source is present.

You do not need to choose the correct medical label before asking for help. Note when the change began, whether it followed an infection, and whether it is constant or comes and goes. Include nasal blockage, pain, new medicines or a head injury rather than assuming every change must be due to COVID-19.

The effect on daily life matters as much as the label. An inability to enjoy meals, discomfort with a partner’s scent or anxiety about detecting hazards can be disruptive even when other symptoms have settled.

Why published percentages vary so much

Studies have asked different questions at different times: some combine smell and taste, some test each sense separately, and others rely on a person’s report. Results soon after infection are not directly comparable with results months later. Recruitment and the virus period also affect who is represented.

For example, the replacement 2023 taste-loss review combined 235 studies from 2020–2021 and estimated a pooled prevalence of about 37%. That historical estimate is not a current infection risk or a prediction of persistent symptoms. The original version of the review was retracted and replaced; its earlier figures should not be used interchangeably with the revision.

Separate early reports of high immediate symptom rates and lower later rates do not form one recovery curve. Nor can a study limited to people with prolonged illness tell us the likelihood for everyone who catches the infection. Ask what a number measures before applying it to your own situation.

Age and sex do not provide a reliable personal forecast

Early research explored whether symptom reports differed by age and sex. Such group patterns cannot tell an individual whether they will lose smell or taste, how severely they will be affected or when they will recover. Different testing methods and participant groups can change an apparent association.

The idea that women must lose more taste because they have “more to lose” is not an established explanation. Likewise, a middle-aged group reporting more symptoms in a study does not make younger or older people protected. Studies with a limited adult age range cannot automatically describe children or the oldest adults.

For care, your actual symptoms, duration and ability to eat are more useful than placing yourself in a supposed low-risk demographic group. A mild original infection also does not make a persistent sensory change imaginary or unimportant.

What genetic and inflammation research can tell us

A genetic association study identified a signal near UGT2A1 and UGT2A2, genes involved in processing odour-related substances. The outcome combined self-reported smell or taste loss. This offers a clue to biology, not proof that either gene alone determines the symptom or a reason to order a consumer genetic test.

Researchers have also studied inflammation and changes in the olfactory system using human samples and animal models, including hamsters. These experiments help investigate how an infection might disrupt sensory tissue and recovery. An animal finding is not the same as demonstrating the mechanism in every affected person.

These lines of research do not establish one explanation for all long-COVID symptoms or identify a guaranteed treatment. A proposed mechanism, an association and a treatment shown to help patients are different kinds of evidence.

Recovery has no guaranteed deadline

Many people improve over weeks or months, but some have symptoms for considerably longer. Improvement can be uneven: an odour may become detectable before it smells familiar again. A change in perception does not by itself tell you whether recovery is complete.

A statement that most patients recover by six months cannot promise that an individual will do so or mean that further improvement is impossible later. Avoid judging yourself against another person’s experience. The starting illness, sensory problem and follow-up period may be different.

If smell has not returned to normal after a few weeks, arrange a primary-care assessment. Seek help sooner if eating or drinking is becoming difficult, you are losing weight, or new symptoms are concerning. Keeping a brief record can make the appointment more useful without repeatedly testing yourself throughout the day.

Assessment and treatment depend on the cause

A clinician may review your infection history, medicines and nasal symptoms, examine the nose and mouth and consider ENT referral or sensory testing. Allergy, sinus disease, nasal polyps and other causes can coexist with a previous COVID infection. Finding a treatable contributor can change the plan.

There is no medicine that reliably restores every post-COVID smell or taste problem. That does not mean no care is available: treatment of an identified nasal condition, rehabilitation advice and nutritional support may be useful. Do not stop a prescribed medicine solely because it appears on a list of possible causes.

Avoid buying a supplement or procedure because it promises to reset damaged nerves. Discuss the evidence, risks, cost and practical goals with your clinician. If you are pregnant, breastfeeding or taking other medicines, include that information before trying a remedy.

Smell training uses short, gentle practice

Smell training involves regularly focusing on a small set of familiar, distinct, safe scents. A hospital leaflet suggests examples such as rose, lemon, clove and eucalyptus, with gentle inhalation for roughly ten seconds at a time and rests between scents. Coffee or other familiar household aromas may be easier to recognise and obtain.

Practice is usually repeated daily over weeks to months; one published hospital approach recommends twice daily and at least four weeks with a group of odours. Follow the programme your clinician recommends. There is no need to force deep inhalations for five to ten minutes or replace all scents every week.

Think about the remembered scent while gently smelling it. Keep concentrated oils away from the inside of the nose, eyes and mouth, and do not swallow them. Avoid irritants, smoke or anything that triggers symptoms, keep products out of children’s reach, and stop if the exercise causes discomfort. Training may help, but is not a guaranteed cure.

Make meals manageable while recovery continues

If an aroma is unpleasant, try a different food with a similar nutritional role rather than abandoning a whole food group. Temperature and texture may change how tolerable a meal feels. Small, manageable portions can be less daunting than a large plate when appetite is low.

Notice whether you are eating much less or compensating with increasing amounts of salt or sugar. Seek advice if your intake is restricted, your weight changes unintentionally or you struggle to stay hydrated. A dietitian can help you maintain variety and adequate nutrition while working around triggers.

Explain specific difficulties to the people sharing meals with you. “That cooking smell is unpleasant to me now” is clearer than forcing yourself to eat something distressing. The aim is a workable eating pattern, not a test of willpower.

Plan for hazards and emotional wellbeing

Do not rely on your nose alone to detect spoiled food, smoke or a gas leak. Maintain working smoke and appropriate gas alarms, follow food storage and use-by guidance, and ask another person for help when needed. Never taste a suspect food to decide whether it is safe.

Persistent sensory changes can affect mood, social life and enjoyment. Tell your clinician if frustration, anxiety or low mood is building. Support is appropriate even when the problem is not visible to others.

At a follow-up, bring a short account of what has changed, which foods or scents are manageable and which daily tasks are affected. Review progress and the next step together. You do not have to wait for a research breakthrough before seeking practical help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Smell and taste are distinct senses, and either can be affected.

Early-pandemic research estimates do not predict your current personal risk or recovery time.

Persistent symptoms deserve assessment and practical support.

How BeMama can help

Keep a short note of sensory changes, food difficulties and household safety concerns to discuss at your next appointment.

When to seek help

Arrange assessment if smell has not returned after a few weeks. Get help sooner if you cannot maintain food or fluid intake, lose weight or develop concerning new symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Mild COVID-19 can still be followed by sensory problems.
  • A loss of flavour is not always a loss of basic taste.
  • Smell training is gentle practice, not prolonged forceful sniffing.
  • Check food and household safety without relying on smell alone.
  • No age, sex or genetic finding guarantees a particular outcome.

Frequently asked questions

Can this happen after a mild infection?

Yes. Sensory symptoms can follow a mild illness as well as a more severe one.

Is bland food proof that I have lost taste?

No. Reduced aroma can make food seem bland even when basic tastes remain detectable.

Why does coffee now smell unpleasant?

Distorted perception of an actual smell is called parosmia; describe the change to your clinician.

Does the 37% figure predict my risk today?

No. It comes from early-pandemic studies and does not predict present-day or individual risk.

Was the original taste-loss review replaced?

Yes. The journal retracted and replaced the original version in 2023; the revised review is the appropriate research reference.

Can a genetic test tell me when I will recover?

No validated recovery forecast follows from the genetic association described here.

Should I wait six months before asking for help?

No. Seek assessment if smell has not returned after a few weeks, or sooner if eating or wellbeing is affected.

Should I sniff oils deeply for several minutes?

No. Smell training uses short, gentle exposures with rests; follow a suitable clinical programme.

Do smell-training scents need changing every week?

No universal weekly schedule is required. Programmes often keep a scent group for several weeks.

What if food restriction is affecting my weight?

Ask for clinical and dietetic support rather than trying to manage prolonged inadequate intake alone.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
